title: HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings)
summary: HyDE asks a model to write a hypothetical answer, embeds that answer instead of the question, and retrieves the real documents nearest to it.
useIf: Queries are short or phrased unlike the documents, you have no relevance labels to fine-tune with, and the model knows the domain.
avoidIf: The domain is proprietary or full of identifiers the model would invent, or the latency budget cannot absorb a generation before retrieval.

explain.md: A short question and a long answer passage often land far apart in embedding space. **HyDE** closes the gap. An instruction-following model writes a **hypothetical document** that answers the query. This text may contain false details. A contrastive encoder embeds it, and the nearest real documents are retrieved. The encoder acts as a filter, because its compressed representation drops fabricated specifics and keeps the topical shape. The method works zero-shot, without relevance labels [[r14]].

explain.title: HyDE request path
explain.alt: The user query goes to a model that writes a hypothetical answer, which is embedded and used to search the index, returning real documents.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant L as LLM
  participant E as Encoder
  participant I as Vector index
  U->>L: Question
  L->>E: Hypothetical answer
  E->>I: Answer vector
  I-->>U: Real documents

explain.md: **When it helps.** Short or vague queries over a domain the model understands, where documents are explanatory prose and the retriever has not been fine-tuned. **When it misleads.** If the model lacks domain knowledge, the hypothetical answer describes the wrong thing and retrieval confidently follows it. For identifiers, SKUs or internal names the model will invent plausible but wrong strings, and a dense encoder will chase them. The Azure Architecture Center names HyDE among query translation methods, next to rewriting and decomposition [[r8]].

**Cost.** It adds a serial generation, of a paragraph, before any retrieval. In practice teams limit the hypothetical text to a short length (author suggestion) and keep the original query on the keyword leg, so a hallucinated hypothetical only affects the vector leg. Evaluate against a baseline of the plain query embedding and a baseline of the plain query plus a rewrite.

explain.title: Why the fake answer is useful
explain.md: The goal is not a correct answer. It is a vector that sits where relevant documents sit. Answer-shaped text is closer to answer passages than a question is, even when its facts are wrong [[r14]].

whereToUse: Zero-shot retrieval over a new corpus with no labelled queries
Scientific or public-domain explanatory content that the model already knows
Short, underspecified questions where the embedding of the question alone is poor
Experiments to estimate headroom before investing in a fine-tuned retriever

use: No relevance labels exist for fine-tuning
Queries are short and documents are long explanatory prose
The model knows the subject area
Latency allows an extra generation before search
avoid: Exact identifiers, SKUs or internal terms dominate
The model has never seen the domain
You have not compared it to a plain-query baseline
flips: The corpus is proprietary: ground the hypothetical text with a first-pass retrieval or skip HyDE
Identifier queries appear: run the original query on a BM25 leg and fuse
Labelled data arrives: fine-tune or adapt the retriever instead of generating on every query

pitfalls.symptom: Retrieval follows an invented product name
pitfalls.cause: The hypothetical document contained a plausible but wrong entity and the encoder matched it
pitfalls.fix: Keep the original query on a keyword leg, or skip HyDE for identifier-shaped queries

pitfalls.symptom: Results are on the wrong topic for niche questions
pitfalls.cause: The model misunderstood the domain, so the hypothetical answer points elsewhere
pitfalls.fix: Add retrieved context to the hypothesis prompt, or use a rewrite instead

pitfalls.cause: Every query pays for a generation, including those the plain embedding handles
pitfalls.fix: Route only short or low-confidence queries through HyDE

scenarios.title: Zero-shot search over a public science corpus
scenarios.situation: A team indexes open-access review articles. Users ask short questions such as 'why do vaccines need boosters'. There are no labelled queries and no budget to fine-tune.
constraints: A few seconds of latency is fine
unknowns: Can you test on a small labelled sample?
scenarios.question: How do you improve retrieval?

options.name: Try HyDE for the vector leg, keep the original on BM25 and compare recall on a small hand-labelled sample
options.why: Short queries against explanatory prose are HyDE's target, the model knows the domain and the keyword leg guards against bad hypotheticals.
options.tradeoff: An extra generation per query and a sample you must label.

options.name: Fine-tune an embedding model
options.why: There are no labelled pairs and the budget is small.
options.tradeoff: Right once you have thousands of labelled pairs in a stable domain.

options.name: Ship plain query embeddings
options.why: Zero added cost and a fair baseline.
options.tradeoff: Short questions embed poorly against long passages.

flips.if: HyDE shows no recall lift on the sample
flips.then: Keep the plain embedding and drop the generation cost.

flips.if: The domain is niche and the model often writes confident but wrong hypothetical answers
flips.then: Skip HyDE: a wrong draft pulls retrieval toward wrong passages, so use plain embeddings or a fine-tuned embedder.

scenarios.takeaway: HyDE shines on short queries in domains the model knows.

scenarios.title: Internal engineering knowledge base
scenarios.situation: Queries mention internal service names and ticket ids. The model has never seen these services.
constraints: Latency under a second for retrieval
unknowns: How often do queries lack identifiers?
scenarios.question: Is HyDE a good fit?

options.name: No. Use hybrid retrieval and rewrite only conversational follow-ups
options.why: The model would invent plausible service behaviour, and exact names belong on a keyword leg.
options.tradeoff: Pure paraphrase questions get less help.

options.name: HyDE on every query
options.why: It adds latency and hallucinated seeds around unknown names.

options.name: HyDE seeded with retrieved snippets
options.tradeoff: It needs a first retrieval, so latency and complexity rise.

flips.if: Queries become long natural-language descriptions with few names
flips.then: Test HyDE again on that slice.

flips.if: The retrieval latency budget loosens to several seconds
flips.then: A generation step becomes affordable, but still gate HyDE on measured recall for the vector leg only.

scenarios.takeaway: Unknown vocabulary breaks the hypothetical document.

quiz.q: In HyDE, what is embedded and used to search the index?
quiz.explain: HyDE embeds a generated hypothetical document. The encoder discards fabricated details, and the nearest real documents are returned [[r14]]. The other options are different techniques.

quiz.q: Which change most clearly argues against HyDE?
options: The corpus uses internal service names the model has never seen
quiz.explain: Unknown vocabulary leads the model to invent specifics, and the encoder chases them. No labels and short queries actually favour HyDE.

quiz.q: Select the costs or risks of HyDE.
options: Hypothetical text may contain false details
It can mislead if the model lacks domain knowledge
quiz.explain: HyDE adds generation latency, may invent details and misleads when the model lacks the domain. It is zero-shot, so it needs no labels [[r14]].

flashcards.back: A hypothetical answer written by a model, not the question. Nearest real documents are then retrieved.

flashcards.front: Why can a false hypothetical document still retrieve well?
flashcards.back: The encoder compresses the text and drops fabricated specifics, keeping a vector near relevant passages.

flashcards.front: Name a safe way to use HyDE next to identifiers.
flashcards.back: Use the hypothetical text only on the vector leg and keep the original query on the BM25 leg.
